description: Greek and Roman temple design — the three architectural orders and the great temples of the classical world.
content_html:
What Was a Temple For?

When a Greek or Roman worshipper approached a temple, they were not entering a place of communal prayer in the way a modern churchgoer might. The cella — the inner room — was the private home of the god, accessible mainly to priests. Worshippers gathered outside at the altar, which stood in the open air in front of the east-facing entrance. The temple’s primary function was to provide a magnificent dwelling for the deity and to house the cult statue. Its grandeur was itself an act of worship, a visible statement of piety and civic pride.

Key Fact

A Greek temple typically consisted of three zones: the pronaos (entrance porch), the cella (inner chamber housing the cult statue), and sometimes an opisthodomos (rear porch, often used as a treasury). The altar stood outside the temple entirely, always to the east.

The Three Architectural Orders

Greek architects developed three distinct systems of design, each identified primarily by the style of its column and capital. The Doric order is the oldest and most austere. Its columns rise directly from the temple platform with no base, taper upward and are crowned by a plain, circular capital topped by a square slab. The overall effect is one of weight and power. The Ionic order is lighter and more elegant. Ionic columns stand on a moulded base, and their capitals are decorated with a pair of distinctive scroll-like spirals called volutes. The Corinthian order, rarely used on Greek temple exteriors but popular in the Roman world, features tall, slender columns and elaborately carved capitals decorated with acanthus leaves.

Greek architects generally used a single order throughout a building. They placed the greatest temples — including the Parthenon and the Temple of Zeus at Olympia — in the Doric order, reflecting a preference for strength and solemnity. Roman architects were bolder about mixing orders and developed the Composite capital, blending Ionic volutes with Corinthian acanthus leaves. Roman temples also typically raised the building on a high podium, so that the dramatic frontal staircase became the only point of entry — very different from Greek temples, which could be approached from all four sides.

This difference reflects a shift in the role of the building. Roman temples were often embedded in a forum or public space where the frontal view was what mattered. Greek temples, set on open hillsides or sanctuaries, were meant to be seen from all angles and were integrated into the landscape.

The Parthenon

The Parthenon, built on the Acropolis at Athens between 447 and 432 BC, is the supreme example of Doric architecture. Constructed from Pentelic marble, it measures approximately 70 metres long and 31 metres wide. Eight columns stand across each of the short ends and seventeen along each long side, creating a peristyle — a colonnade running all the way around the building. The outer columns are slightly thicker at the middle (a technique called entasis) to prevent an optical illusion of inward curvature.

Inside the cella stood the colossal chryselephantine statue of Athena Parthenos, crafted by the sculptor Pheidias. The statue was approximately 12 metres tall and made of ivory for the flesh and gold sheeting for the drapery and armour — a display of enormous wealth. The Parthenon also housed the city’s treasury and was adorned with extensive sculptural programmes: the mythological battles on the metopes, the continuous frieze around the inner colonnade, and the pedimental groups at east and west ends.

Key Fact

The Parthenon (447–432 BC) is a Doric temple on the Athenian Acropolis, dedicated to Athena. It had 8 columns on the short ends and 17 along the sides. Its architects were Iktinos and Kallikrates; the sculptural programme was overseen by Pheidias, who also created the 12-metre ivory-and-gold cult statue inside.

The Temple of Zeus at Olympia

The Temple of Zeus at Olympia, completed around 457 BC, was one of the largest Doric temples in Greece. Built from local limestone coated in stucco, it had 6 columns at each end and 13 along each side. Inside stood another chryselephantine masterpiece by Pheidias — the seated Zeus, regarded in antiquity as one of the Seven Wonders of the World. The temple’s exterior sculptural programme was also significant: the metopes above the porch depicted the Twelve Labours of Heracles, directly connecting the sanctuary to Heracles as the founder of the Olympic Games.

Roman Temples: The Pantheon and the Temple of Fortuna Virilis

The Pantheon in Rome, rebuilt by the emperor Hadrian around AD 125, is extraordinary because it combines a traditional Corinthian-columned porch with a vast circular rotunda. The rotunda is covered by a concrete dome 43 metres in diameter — the same measurement as its height — with a circular opening at the top called the oculus, approximately 9 metres across. Light from the oculus moves slowly across the interior throughout the day, creating an awe-inspiring effect. The Pantheon was dedicated to all the gods and has survived almost entirely intact to the present day, largely because it was converted into a Christian church in 609 AD.

The Temple of Fortuna Virilis (now identified as the Temple of Portunus), overlooking the Tiber in Rome, is one of the best-preserved Republican-era temples. Built in the late 2nd or early 1st century BC, it stands on a high podium accessed by steps at the front only. It uses the Ionic order, with four free-standing columns at the front and engaged columns (columns built into the wall) along the sides — a feature typical of Roman architecture, creating the illusion of a full colonnade while saving material and space. This engaged-column design is distinctly Roman and distinguishes it clearly from Greek peripteral temples.

Students sometimes imagine Greek and Roman temples as functioning like a church, mosque or synagogue — a space where congregations gathered inside for communal worship. This is a misconception. The cella was restricted, and the main acts of worship (sacrifice, prayer, offerings) happened outside at the altar. The interior was the god’s private home. An ancient Greek would have found the idea of a congregation sitting inside the god’s house deeply strange.

This difference matters for answering source questions: when you describe a temple, always note the relationship between the outdoor altar (where worship happened), the inner cella (where the cult statue lived), and the role of the priests who mediated between the two.
exam_tip_html: The command word Describe asks you to give an account of what is there — for architecture questions, name specific features (Doric columns, cella, podium, oculus) and say what they look like or where they are. Do not just say “it was impressive.” For Explain questions about why a building was designed as it was, connect the physical feature to its purpose: for example, the Pantheon’s oculus allowed light into a building that had no windows, while also symbolising the open eye of heaven. For source-analysis questions, use specific details in the source rather than general knowledge — if the question gives you a description of the Parthenon’s columns, use those details in your answer.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Greek temples served as the god’s home, not a congregational space. The altar was outside; the cella housed the cult statue and was largely inaccessible to ordinary worshippers.
  • The three architectural orders (Doric, Ionic, Corinthian) can be identified by their columns and capitals; the Parthenon and Temple of Zeus at Olympia are Doric, while the Pantheon uses Corinthian and the Temple of Portunus uses Ionic.
  • Roman temple design differs from Greek in three key ways: the high podium with frontal staircase, the use of engaged columns along the sides, and the greater use of concrete, allowing extraordinary forms such as the Pantheon’s dome.

practice_questions.text: Name the architectural order used in the construction of the Parthenon.
Describe the main features of the cella of a Greek temple.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of the following: the cella was the inner chamber of the temple; it housed the cult statue of the god; it was generally inaccessible to ordinary worshippers; it was entered through the pronaos (entrance porch); it could contain a treasury; it was surrounded on the outside by columns (peristyle).

practice_questions.text: Read the following description of a famous Roman temple: a massive circular building entered through a Corinthian-columned porch, its interior covered by a concrete dome of exactly equal height and diameter, with a circular hole open to the sky at its very centre. What does this architectural design suggest about the Romans' attitude towards the gods and their skill as builders? Use details from the description in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): Precise reference to specific details in the description (dome, oculus, Corinthian porch, equal height and diameter) with sustained analysis of what each implies; the circular oculus linked to the open eye of heaven or the all-seeing gods; the dome's mathematical perfection linked to divine order; the concrete construction linked to Roman engineering ambition. A clear judgement about what the combination reveals.
Secure (3-4): Two or three specific details used analytically with some explanation of significance.
Developing (2): One or two details mentioned with limited analysis.
Emerging (1): General description without engaging with the source details.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the altar was placed outside a Greek or Roman temple rather than inside it.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any four of the following developed points: the cella was the god's private dwelling and worship happened in the god's presence outside; the altar was the site of animal sacrifice which required open air (smoke, fire, blood); crowds could not fit inside the restricted cella; the altar faced east so the sacrificing priest could look towards the rising sun; the god's statue stood inside as the permanent resident while the community gathered outside; Roman temples on a podium with frontal steps meant the altar directly faced the entrance steps.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the Parthenon is the greatest achievement of Greek architecture? Use named sources and a balanced argument in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9-10): Sustained argument engaging with the Parthenon's specific features (Doric order, entasis, Pheidias' cult statue, sculptural programme, Pentelic marble) alongside comparison with at least one other major Greek structure; balanced view considering what makes architecture 'greatest' (innovation, beauty, scale, religious function); judgement clearly supported by named sources.
Secure (6-8): Clear argument with reference to the Parthenon's features and at least one comparator; some awareness of different criteria; evidence cited.
Developing (3-5): Some relevant points about the Parthenon with limited comparison or limited source use.
Emerging (1-2): Simple descriptive points; little or no argument or source use.

practice_questions.text: Explain two key differences between Greek and Roman temple design.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two clearly explained differences (e.g. Greek peripteral colonnade vs Roman engaged columns + podium; Greek temples approachable from all sides vs Roman frontal entrance; use of concrete and dome in Rome vs marble column-and-lintel in Greece) with specific named examples for each (Parthenon / Temple of Portunus / Pantheon) and a clear sense of what the difference reveals about each culture's priorities.
Secure (3-4): Two differences identified and explained with some evidence but analysis less developed.
Developing (1-2): One difference stated or two superficially mentioned.

knowledge_checks.q: Which architectural order is used in the construction of the Parthenon?
What is the oculus of the Pantheon?
options: The high platform on which a Roman temple stands
The circular opening at the top of the dome that lets in light
The scroll-shaped decoration on an Ionic capital
The entrance porch of a Greek temple

knowledge_checks.q: The inner chamber of a Greek temple that housed the cult statue was called the _____.
The Ionic order is distinguished from the Doric by its slender columns and capital decorated with paired scroll-like spirals called _____.
Match each temple to its correct description:
right: Doric temple on the Athenian Acropolis, dedicated to Athena
Roman rotunda with a concrete dome and circular oculus, dedicated to all the gods
Ionic Roman temple on a podium with engaged columns along its sides

flashcard_questions.q: What is the cella of a Greek temple?
flashcard_questions.a: The inner chamber housing the cult statue, largely off-limits to ordinary worshippers.

flashcard_questions.q: Where was the altar positioned in relation to a Greek temple?
flashcard_questions.a: Outside the temple, to the east, in front of the entrance.

flashcard_questions.q: What distinguishes a Doric column from an Ionic column?
flashcard_questions.a: Doric has a plain capital and no base; Ionic has a moulded base and volute (scroll) capitals.
Scroll-shaped spiral decorations that form the distinctive capital of the Ionic order.

flashcard_questions.q: What is entasis in Greek architecture?
flashcard_questions.a: A subtle outward curve on columns to prevent the optical illusion that straight lines bow inward.

flashcard_questions.q: Which architectural order was used for the Parthenon, built between 447 and 432 BC?
flashcard_questions.a: The Doric order — the oldest and most austere of the three Greek orders.

flashcard_questions.q: What was inside the cella of the Parthenon?
flashcard_questions.a: A colossal chryselephantine (gold and ivory) statue of Athena by the sculptor Pheidias.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the oculus of the Pantheon?
flashcard_questions.a: A circular opening 9 metres across at the top of the dome, the only source of natural light.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the Pantheon's dome measurement relate to its height?
flashcard_questions.a: The dome's diameter and the building's interior height are equal — both approximately 43 metres.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a podium in Roman temple architecture?
flashcard_questions.a: A high platform raising the temple above street level, with steps only at the front.

flashcard_questions.q: What architectural feature distinguishes the Temple of Portunus from a Greek temple?
flashcard_questions.a: Engaged columns (built into the wall) along the sides rather than a free-standing peristyle.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the sculptor who oversaw the Parthenon's sculptural programme and created the cult statue.

glossary_terms.definition: The inner chamber of a Greek or Roman temple that housed the cult statue of the god.
The simplest and most massive of the three Greek architectural orders, characterised by a plain capital and heavy, fluted columns with no base.
A Greek architectural order characterised by slender columns with a base and a capital decorated with paired scroll-like spirals called volutes.
Scroll-shaped decorative spiral elements that form the distinctive feature of an Ionic capital.
A subtle convex curve built into the columns and stepped platform of a Greek temple to counteract the optical illusion that perfectly straight lines appear to curve inward.
A high platform or base on which a Roman temple stood, raising it above street level and accessible only from the front.
A Roman temple in Rome dedicated to all the gods, notable for its enormous concrete dome with a central oculus open to the sky.
A circular opening at the top of the Pantheon's dome, 9 metres in diameter, which provides the building's only natural light.
